questions.text: In a control-flow graph, what does it mean for block d to dominate block b?

options.A: Every path from the function entry to b passes through d.
options.B: Block d has a numerically lower address than block b.
options.C: Block d has more outgoing edges than block b.
options.D: At least one path from the entry to d passes through b.

questions.explanation: Dominance is an all-paths property from the entry. Address order and edge count do not establish it.

questions.text: An unconditional jump skips four table bytes, but linear sweep decodes those bytes and starts an instruction one byte before the jump target. What should you do?

options.A: Accept the sweep because every byte produced a valid mnemonic.
options.B: Remove the jump target because it conflicts with the sweep listing.
options.C: Follow the jump from the known entry and decode at its actual target.
options.D: Mark the function unreachable because it contains an embedded table.

questions.explanation: A sweep can absorb data bytes into plausible instructions. Recursive descent follows the control-flow target and avoids the skipped data on this path.

questions.text: For a conditional branch, recursive_descent appends target to worklist, then sets address = instruction.end. With target=0x80, instruction.end=0x24, and an initially empty worklist, what is the resulting state?
questions.explanation: append queues 0x80 for later. Assigning instruction.end makes the current traversal continue at fallthrough 0x24.
